root_cause.text: `nvme_poll_irqdisable()` in the NVMe PCI driver recomputed the IRQ number twice from `pci_irq_vector(pdev, nvmeq->cq_vector)`, so a concurrent reset/disable could change `pdev->msix_enabled` between `disable_irq()` and `enable_irq()`, causing the two calls to act on different IRQs and trigger unbalanced IRQ accounting.
root_cause.evidence: The patch changes `disable_irq(pci_irq_vector(...))` / `enable_irq(pci_irq_vector(...))` to store `irq = pci_irq_vector(pdev, nvmeq->cq_vector);` and use that same local `irq` for both calls; the CVE description says `nvme_reset_work()->nvme_dev_disable()` can set `pdev->msix_enabled = 0` between those calls, making `pci_irq_vector()` return MSI-X IRQ for the first call and INTx IRQ for the second, which led to “Unbalanced enable for IRQ 10.”

intent_record.intent_summary: Cache the PCI IRQ vector in nvme_poll_irqdisable() and reuse it for disable/enable operations.
intent_record.what: In nvme_poll_irqdisable(), a new local variable 'int irq' was added. The code now stores the result of pci_irq_vector(pdev, nvmeq->cq_vector) in 'irq' once, then passes 'irq' to disable_irq() and enable_irq() instead of calling pci_irq_vector() twice inline.
intent_record.how: At runtime, the interrupt vector is resolved a single time and reused for both disabling and enabling the IRQ. This avoids repeating the lookup and ensures the same IRQ value is used for both operations within the function call.

grouping_result.intent: Cache the PCI IRQ vector in nvme_poll_irqdisable() and reuse it for disable/enable operations.

relevance_review.reason: The change directly matches the root cause: it fixes nvme_poll_irqdisable() recomputing the IRQ vector twice by caching the PCI IRQ number and reusing it for both disable_irq() and enable_irq(), preventing mismatched IRQ accounting during concurrent reset/disable.

candidates.rationale: This call computes the IRQ vector directly at the time of disable; if `pdev->msix_enabled` changes before the later enable path, it may disable one IRQ while the matching enable targets another, creating unbalanced IRQ accounting.
This call recomputes the IRQ vector instead of reusing the one used for `disable_irq()`, so a concurrent reset/disable can make the enable operate on a different IRQ than was disabled.

vuln_statements.explanation: This statement computes the IRQ vector at the time of disable, which can differ from the later enable if `pdev->msix_enabled` changes concurrently, leading to mismatched IRQ accounting.
This statement recomputes the IRQ vector instead of reusing the one disabled earlier, so a concurrent reset/disable can cause enable to act on a different IRQ and unbalance IRQ state.

Author: Keith Busch <kbusch@kernel.org>

    nvme-pci: Simplify nvme_poll_irqdisable
    
    The timeout handler can use the existing nvme_poll() if it needs to
    check a polled queue, allowing nvme_poll_irqdisable() to handle only
    irq driven queues for the remaining callers.
    
    Signed-off-by: Keith Busch <kbusch@kernel.org>

diff --git a/drivers/nvme/host/pci.c b/drivers/nvme/host/pci.c
index 02f2
bic_trace_step.reason: The vulnerable construct is not present in this snippet. The root cause was that nvme_poll_irqdisable() handled both polled and interrupt-driven queues and could recompute the IRQ twice around disable_irq()/enable_irq(). In this commit, the function was simplified to only handle interrupt-driven queues: it now contains `WARN_ON_ONCE(test_bit(NVMEQ_POLLED, &nvmeq->flags));` and always executes `disable_irq(pci_irq_vector(pdev, nvmeq->cq_vector)); ... enable_irq(pci_irq_vector(pdev, nvmeq->cq_vector));` without the old polled-queue branch. The timeout path also avoids calling this function for polled queues: `if (test_bit(NVMEQ_POLLED, &nvmeq->flags)) nvme_poll(req->mq_hctx); else nvme_poll_irqdisable(nvmeq);`. This shows the fix is already present in the shown code, and the prior vulnerable logic is absent.
